aml.pepTooltip: A politically exposed person (PEP) is someone who currently or in the past  has been entrusted with a prominent public function. That includes  head of state or head of government, government minister or member of parliament, important political party officials, supreme court member, member of the board of the central bank or state comptroller, ambassador, senior military officials, senior executives or members of the board of state owned corporations or international organisations. Relatives of PEPs include their spouse or person deemed equivalent to a spouse, parents, children and their spouse or persons deemed equivalent to a spouse. Close associates of PEPs include individuals who co-own a company or have any legal connection with a PEP or are in close business relations with a PEP. Persons with beneficial ownership of legal entities or arrangements known to have been founded for the benefit of a PEP are also considered close associates.

secondPillarTaxWin.calculationDetails.ti: How exactly does this calculation work?
secondPillarTaxWin.calculationDetails.pa: Up to 6% of your gross salary is paid to the II pillar monthly, based on your chosen contribution. The chart columns show your actual payments to the II pillar during {currentYear} and calculate what the payments would have been with higher or lower contributions.

Since contributions are made from gross salary before income tax withholding, II pillar payments are income tax-free. For example, if your salary is 2000 € and your contribution is 2%, then 40 € per month goes to your II pillar. Of this, 31.2 € comes from net salary and 8.8 € from income tax. However, if your contribution were 6%, then 120 € per month would go to your II pillar, of which 26.4 € is income tax benefit.

By increasing II pillar payments, you can get up to three times greater tax benefit per year. With a 2000 € salary example, the saver earns 345 € in tax benefits, which goes to grow in their II pillar.

Additionally, 4% of gross salary is paid to the II pillar from social tax. For a 2000 € monthly salary, this is 80 €. This doesn't depend on the saver's contribution. Social tax paid to the II pillar <link>affects the I pillar to a small extent</link>. The calculation may be incorrect for you if you have been on parental leave this year.

pensionCalculator.how.withdrawal.body: A fund pension sells the same number of units every month while the rest of the money keeps earning a return. That is why the monthly payment grows over time as the fund's value rises.
pensionCalculator.how.tax.heading: Tax
pensionCalculator.how.tax.body: Monthly payments from the II and III pillar are free of income tax if you spread them over at least the years Statistikaamet expects someone starting at that age to still live. Over a shorter period the income tax is 10%. For the investment fund we assume an investment account: 22% income tax applies once the amount taken out exceeds what was paid in. Taxation depends on your individual circumstances, including residency, and tax laws change over time. Check your exact payout period with Pensionikeskus.

futureMe.you.faq.intro.q: What is Future Me and who is it for?
futureMe.you.faq.intro.a:
Future Me calculates how much pension assets you will have in total at retirement age, and how long they cover your costs. You see your decisions year by year up to retirement age and after it: when to retire, and how to use the state pension and the pillar assets.

It is for anyone who wants to understand, before retiring, what the different choices mean for them. The result is a calculation based on your data and assumptions, not a promise or a forecast of returns.
futureMe.you.faq.pillars.q: What are the state pension and the II and III pillar?
futureMe.you.faq.pillars.a:
The state pension (I pillar) is a monthly amount guaranteed by the state. It builds up from the social tax your employer pays on your salary (33%, of which 20% goes to pension insurance). Every year you work increases it.

The II pillar receives part of your salary (2%, 4% or 6%), and the state adds 4% of your salary from the social tax. That is why the state pension of a II pillar member is smaller.

In the III pillar you make voluntary contributions yourself. You get income tax back on up to 15% of your gross income, but no more than €6,000 a year.

The II and III pillar assets are yours and pass to your heirs. The state pension is not part of an estate.
futureMe.you.faq.pensionAge.q: What are the retirement age and the flexible pension?
futureMe.you.faq.pensionAge.a:
The retirement age is the age from which you get the old-age state pension in full. Today it is 65 years, and it will rise as people live longer. In the You step we show your retirement age based on the Tuleva pension calculator forecast, and you can change it.

The flexible pension means you choose when to start the state pension:

  • Earlier: up to 5 years before the retirement age. The pension is then smaller for life.
  • Later: the longer you postpone it, the larger the pension is for life.
  • Half: you take half of the pension and the other half keeps growing, as if you had postponed it.
futureMe.you.faq.kids.q: Why do I need to add my children?
futureMe.you.faq.kids.a:
Children can increase your pension and let you retire earlier:

  • Pension supplement: you get it for a child you have raised for at least 8 years.
  • II pillar additional contribution: for a child born in 2013 or later, the state pays a contribution into the II pillar of one parent who is a II pillar member, instead of the pension supplement, until the child turns 3. It depends on the age of the child, not on the 8 years.
  • Retiring earlier: if you have raised three or more children, or a child with a disability, for at least 8 years, you can retire earlier without a reduction of your pension.

If you do not add your children, we do not count them.
futureMe.you.faq.special.q: What are work-related special cases and why do they matter?
futureMe.you.faq.special.a:
For some jobs and offices the law has exceptions: you can retire earlier, get a separate pension or a larger pension. Tick the ones that apply to you:

  • health-damaging work;
  • special pension (e.g. police, defense forces, prosecution);
  • rescue service;
  • civil servant service years;
  • other special case.

Each case is explained under its “?”. You can check your rights with the Social Insurance Board or your employer.

futureMe.fundPensionFaq.title: Frequently asked questions
futureMe.fundPensionFaq.what.a:
Monthly payouts mean you take your II or III pillar assets out in parts, for example every month. In the law and at Pensionikeskus this is called a funded pension. The assets you have not taken out yet stay in the fund and keep growing.

  • If the payout period is at least as long as your expected remaining lifetime according to Statistics Estonia, the payouts are free of income tax.
  • If you want to spread the money over a longer time, sign a new agreement every year (income-tax-free) or take the money out in parts (10% income tax).
  • The fund units in the fund pass to your heirs.

Read more about pension payouts on the Tuleva website
futureMe.fundPensionFaq.when.q: When should you choose monthly payouts?
futureMe.fundPensionFaq.when.a:
• If you expect a long life. A 65-year-old woman lives another 21.4 years on average (to about 86), a man 16.3 years (to about 81) (Statistics Estonia 2025). That is the average: half live longer, and one woman in ten lives to 97 and one man in ten to 93. When the pillar money runs out, only the state pension is left.
  • A monthly payout agreement can be renewed every year. One agreement lasts for your remaining life expectancy and then ends. If you sign a new agreement every year for the remaining assets (again for your remaining life expectancy), the payouts last longer and stay free of income tax, but at a very old age the monthly payout is smaller.
  • If you have other savings or investments you can live on in your first years of retirement, you can leave the pillar money in the fund to grow and start monthly payouts later.
  • Taking everything out at once is the worst for income tax: the income tax is 10% (22% before that age). For the money you take out to earn as much as in the fund, it would have to earn back the 10% income tax, which means a riskier investment.
  • On a deposit money usually loses value: 22% of the deposit interest goes on income tax and the rest mostly falls short of rising prices. The calculation assumes a deposit loses 1% of its buying power a year (for example, 3% interest, 2.3% after income tax, prices rising 3.3%). This is an assumption, not a forecast. The loss is smaller than if you spent it all, but still a loss.
  • If you have no other savings, the state pension and the III pillar may not last for life. Monthly payouts are then the safest way.

Tuleva’s advice: use your II and III pillar money only when you really need it. Monthly payouts are free of income tax and the money you have not taken out keeps growing in the fund; taking it out at once or in parts has 10% income tax. Insurance contract fees are so high at the moment that Tuleva does not consider it sensible.

Read more about pension payouts on the Tuleva website
futureMe.fundPensionFaq.surplus.q: What if the payouts are bigger than I need?
futureMe.fundPensionFaq.surplus.a:
• The payout does not depend on your costs. The monthly payout is the fund amount divided by the number of payouts still to come (Funded Pensions Act § 60¹ (5)). You cannot choose a smaller amount.
  • The surplus goes to a deposit. In the calculation, money on a deposit loses 1% of its value a year after inflation, while in the fund it keeps growing. If the surplus sits on a deposit for longer than 3–4 years, you lose more than the 10% income tax you would pay if you took out only the amount you need from the fund (“Keep saving”).
  • Monthly payouts can be paused and started again later (see “What should I know about monthly payouts?”). For example, if you postpone your state pension, you can live on monthly payouts in the meantime and pause them when the state pension starts. Future Me does not calculate pausing separately; “Keep saving” or starting monthly payouts later gives a similar result.
futureMe.fundPensionFaq.know.q: What should I know about monthly payouts?
futureMe.fundPensionFaq.know.a:
• An application is enough. You do not need to move the money anywhere: each month a small part of your fund units is sold automatically, and the rest stays in the fund.
  • Period and income tax. The fund manager (e.g. Tuleva) sets the period to your statistical remaining life expectancy (about 19 years for an average 65-year-old). With such a period the payouts are free of income tax. The calculation rounds the period of one agreement to whole years (e.g. 18.56 → 19 years). If your agreement counts in months, the monthly payout can be up to about 2% bigger. For a new agreement every year, the calculation counts the period in months.
  • The money keeps earning a return. For example, if the fund grows 7% a year on average, the payout at the end of the period is more than three times bigger than at the start. The payout goes up and down with the unit price: if the fund grows, so does the payout, and the other way round.
  • Flexible. You can pause monthly payouts at any time and start them again later. If needed, you can also make a partial payout (10% income tax), which reduces later monthly payouts.
  • Contributions. When you start II pillar payouts, your II pillar contributions end for good, including the state’s 4%. You can keep paying into the III pillar even when you already take money from it, and you still get income tax back.
  • Inheritance. Your II and III pillar units in the fund are part of your estate. Your heirs get them on their own pension account or as money (22% income tax); you do not need to apply for this.
futureMe.fundPensionFaq.at60.q: Can monthly payouts start as early as 5 years before retirement age?
futureMe.fundPensionFaq.at60.a:
Yes. II pillar monthly payouts can start up to 5 years before retirement age. If the period is at least the recommended length (your remaining life expectancy according to Statistics Estonia), the payouts are free of income tax. From the III pillar you can get monthly payouts from age 55 (if you joined before 2021) or 5 years before retirement age.

  • Starting payouts ends your II pillar contributions, including the state’s 4%. If you keep working, you lose them.
  • If you start earlier, the period is longer and the monthly payout smaller.
  • Poor health: if you expect a shorter life, starting earlier can make sense, because you get the money when you need it. The income-tax-free period, however, is based on average life expectancy, not your health. If you have no capacity for work at all, you can retire from the II pillar at any age, free of income tax.
futureMe.fundPensionFaq.choose.q: How do you choose a monthly payout agreement?
futureMe.fundPensionFaq.choose.a:
You can take monthly payouts with two kinds of agreement.

  • One agreement. You choose up to what age the payouts last: at least up to your average life expectancy, and then they are free of income tax. A later age means a smaller monthly payout, but the payouts last longer. At the age you chose, the agreement and the payouts end.
  • New agreement every year. Every year the remaining assets are spread again over your average remaining lifetime. The payouts are free of income tax and last longer, but at a very old age the monthly payout is smaller.
  • A period shorter than your average life expectancy is not free of income tax.
futureMe.fundPensionFaq.order.q: Which pillar should I use first?
futureMe.fundPensionFaq.order.a:
If you are still working, the III pillar. Once you start payouts from the II pillar, your II pillar contributions end for good, including the state’s 4%. For example, if you take II pillar payouts, then work less or take a break and later go back to work, the state no longer pays into your II pillar. You can keep paying into the III pillar while taking payouts from it.

If you no longer work and use the assets for your monthly costs, the two pillars are about equal.

futureMe.age65.faq.yearScore.q: What are a yearly rate and a year of service?
futureMe.age65.faq.yearScore.a:
The state pension is calculated in units. Every unit gives the same amount: from 1 April 2026 it is €10.48 a month.

  • A yearly rate shows how much social tax was paid for you in one year. For the Estonian average salary you get 1 yearly rate in a year, for half that salary 0.5. Yearly rates are collected from 1999.
  • A year of service is a working year up to 1998. Each year of service gives as much as 1 yearly rate, whatever your salary.

For example, 3.5 yearly rates for children give 3.5 × €10.48 ≈ €37 a month. Two years of service give 2 × €10.48 ≈ €21 a month.

The children’s pension supplement is a separate right: if it stays with you, it is added to your old-age pension at {pensionAge}. You choose which parent gets the supplement under “Who gets the pension supplement or the II pillar additional contribution?”.

If you raise the children alone, the pension for children from {aloneAges} may be better for you, because it includes the children’s pension supplement straight away.

futureMe.age65.faq.deferral.q: What does postponing your pension or taking half mean?
futureMe.age65.faq.deferral.a:
The state pension is paid to you for the rest of your life. If you start later, it is paid over fewer years, which is why each monthly amount is bigger. The increase stays with you for life.

  • You postpone it: during that time you get no state pension. If you postpone it by 1 year, your pension is {deferred} a month instead of {base}, {extra} more for life.
  • You take half: you get {half} a month straight away. The other half grows like a postponed pension, but only on that half: after 1 year the full amount is {afterHalf} a month. You can switch from a half pension to a full one and back once a month.

When does it pay off? If you postpone it by 1 year, you miss out on {missed}. The bigger pension earns this back in about {paybackYears} years. If you live longer, you get more in total. In the meantime you live on your salary or your II and III pillar money.

The amounts are before income tax. The percentages are the Social Insurance Board’s 2026 averages (+7.93% for 1 year). Your exact percentage depends on your birth month and when your pension is granted. Source: Social Insurance Board: flexible pension.

futureMe.help.sex.title: Why do we ask your sex?
futureMe.help.sex.body:
In Estonia, women live longer than men on average. This affects how many years your money has to last.

Remaining life expectancy (Statistics Estonia, 2025):

AgeMenWomen6065
19.8 years25.8 years
16.3 years21.4 years

Other: the calculation uses Statistics Estonia figures for the whole population, men and women together (19.3 years at 65).

The income-tax-free period for monthly payouts is the same for everyone, whatever your sex: the remaining life expectancy of the whole population according to Statistics Estonia (19.3 years at 65). The Social Insurance Board calculator works the same way.

Life expectancy has grown over the years. From 2027, the retirement age is linked to changes in the life expectancy of 65-year-olds. You will see the age at which you retire in the next steps. The calculation uses the latest life table published by Statistics Estonia (2025) and does not forecast longer lives.

Source: Statistics Estonia RV045 and RV046, life table 2025 (latest published year).
futureMe.help.pensionAge.title: How is the retirement age set?
futureMe.help.pensionAge.body:
Future Me works out your retirement age itself from your birth year and fills in the “Retirement age” field. Only change it if you want to calculate with a different age.

The law (State Pension Insurance Act § 7¹, years 2027–2029): the retirement age is 65 years plus the change in the life expectancy of 65-year-olds. The five-year average life expectancy (4–8 years earlier) is compared with the base period 2018–2022. The retirement age is set to the month, it can rise by at most 3 months a year, and the minister sets it two years in advance.

The retirement age applies by calendar year: your retirement age is the one in force in the year you reach that age.

YearRetirement age2026202720282029later
65 years
65 years 1 month (set)
65 years 3 months (set)
65 years 4 months (set)
forecast: 1.5 months for every birth year after 1962, e.g. born 1980: 67 years, 2000: 70 years

Nobody knows the exact retirement age after 2029. It depends on how long people will live. The retirement age is forecast from Tuleva’s figures, not the Social Insurance Board calculator. Like the Tuleva savings calculator, the calculation assumes the retirement age rises by 1.5 months for every birth year after 1962: the middle of the Ministry of Finance estimate (1–2 months). If the retirement age already set for you is higher, the calculation uses that.

The Social Insurance Board retirement age is usually lower, because its calculator assumes life expectancy stays at the level of the latest published year (2025: 65-year-olds live another 18.9 years on average). To find that age: Social Insurance Board self-service → Calculators → Pension calculator → Forecast → “Retirement”: choose “Old-age pension” and look at “Time of retirement”. Subtract your birth year from that year to get your retirement age. If you want to calculate with the Social Insurance Board age, choose it in the “Retirement age” field.

In the Social Insurance Board calculator, make sure to choose “Old-age pension”, not retiring earlier because of children or health-damaging work. Future Me asks about retiring earlier separately and subtracts those years itself.

Sources: State Pension Insurance Act § 7 and § 7¹, Social Insurance Board: retirement age, Statistics Estonia RV045. Data as of 26 October 2026.
futureMe.help.p1.title: What is the state pension?
futureMe.help.p1.body:
What is the amount here? It is the average old-age pension in 2026: €860 a month before income tax (from 1 April 2026). It is not a forecast of your state pension. If you know your forecast, enter it here.

The old-age state pension (I pillar) is the main income for most pensioners. Its size affects how you get by in retirement more than anything else. Your other savings are not included here.

You can look up your own forecast in the Social Insurance Board pension calculator, section “Forecast”:

  1. Turn on “Take accumulated pension data into account” and enter your gross salary, II pillar contribution and III pillar contribution.
  2. Leave “I have worked in the public service for at least 10 years until 31 March 2018” turned off: Future Me adds the civil servant increase itself if you tick in the You step that you were a civil servant.
  3. Do not add children under “Pension supplement”: Future Me adds the children’s pension supplement itself if you add your children in the You step.
  4. Under “Retirement”, choose “Old-age pension” (not earlier because of children or the flexible pension: Future Me works those out itself).
  5. Open the details next to “Forecast result” and take the “I pillar” line. That amount is before income tax, in today’s euros.

Do not take:

  • the “Forecast result” total: it also includes the II and III pillar, which Future Me works out itself (they would count twice);
  • “Pension accumulated so far” or the I pillar amount in the “Pension pillars” view: that is today’s position without your future working years.

Take the retirement age from Future Me, not the Social Insurance Board calculator: it assumes life expectancy does not grow and so shows a lower age. The forecast assumes your salary stays the same; if your salary changes, work out the forecast again.

How it is made up:

  • Base amount: the same for everyone.
  • Length-of-service part: years worked up to 1998. Each year counts the same; your salary does not matter.
  • Insurance part (1999–2020): based on the social tax paid for you. Twice the salary gives twice as much.
  • Combined part (from 2021): half based on your salary, half equal for everyone. Twice the salary gives about 1.5 times as much.

Seems small for your salary? Since 2021 the state pension depends less on your salary (the combined part). A II pillar member gets a smaller state pension, because 4% of their salary goes to the II pillar. So an older person with many working years before 1999 can get a larger state pension than a younger person with a higher salary. Next to the younger person’s state pension comes the money from the II pillar.

The pension is indexed every year on 1 April. The calculation is in today’s euros, so growth that only keeps up with prices is left out.
futureMe.help.gross.title: How does your salary change in the calculation?
futureMe.help.gross.body:
The calculation assumes your salary rises 3% a year and prices 2% a year (the European Central Bank’s target). In today’s money your salary therefore grows about 1% a year. II pillar contributions (your 2, 4 or 6% and the state’s 4%) are a percentage of your salary, so in today’s money they also grow about 1% a year.

All amounts are in today’s euros.

Source: Tuleva pension calculator, European Central Bank: inflation target of 2%.
futureMe.help.p2Rate.title: What does the II pillar contribution mean?
futureMe.help.p2Rate.body:
• 2% of your gross salary is the default.
  • 4% or 6%: since 2025 you can choose to raise your contribution. It does not reduce your state pension rights.
  • The state adds another 4% of your gross salary to the II pillar (from the social tax), whether you pay 2%, 4% or 6% yourself.
  • None: you have not joined the II pillar or you have left it.

You can change the contribution rate (2%, 4% or 6%) once a year. The new rate applies from January if you apply by 30 November.

Source: Pensionikeskus: changing the contribution rate. Data as of 26 October 2026.

Can you take II pillar money out before retirement age?

  • From 5 years before retirement age you can use the money as a pension: monthly payouts spread over your remaining life expectancy are free of income tax, and taking it all at once has 10% income tax.
  • Earlier you can take the money out with 22% income tax. From 1 November 2026 you can do this only once. Your and the state’s contributions then stop, and you can start again after 5 years (previously 10 years).
  • From 2028 you can also take out part of the money. If you only stopped contributions (without taking money out), you can then start again straight away.
  • Money you take out no longer grows towards your pension and you miss the state’s 4%, so you have less for retirement.
Source: Funded Pensions Act § 27¹, § 27², § 43¹. Data as of 26 October 2026. The changes apply from 1 November 2026 and 1 January 2028.
futureMe.help.p3Monthly.title: How does your III pillar contribution change in the calculation?
futureMe.help.p3Monthly.body:
The calculation assumes you pay the same amount in euros every year into the III pillar. The tax benefit limit is 15% of your gross income, but no more than €6,000 a year, and this limit does not rise with prices. A III pillar contribution is not a percentage of your salary, so it does not grow with your salary like the II pillar contribution (about 1% a year). As prices rise 2% a year, the same amount is about 2% smaller in today’s money every year. This only affects new contributions: the money already in the pillar grows by the return you chose.

If you raise your contribution with prices, your assets grow more. The tax benefit limit (€6,000 a year) is a fixed amount in the law. It may be changed in future as prices rise, but that cannot be known in advance, so the calculation uses the current limit.

Source: Tax and Customs Board: III pillar tax benefit, Tuleva pension calculator.
futureMe.help.p3Joined.title: Why does it matter when you joined the III pillar?
futureMe.help.p3Joined.body:
It decides from what age you can take out all your III pillar money with less income tax (10%, otherwise 22%).

  • Joined before 2021: the lower income tax applies from age 55.
  • Joined in 2021 or later: the lower income tax applies from 5 years before retirement age, as for the II pillar.

Less income tax means 10% income tax if you take all the money out at once, and 0% as monthly payouts. Before that age the income tax is 22%. You must have been saving for at least 5 years.

Where to see when you joined:

  • In the Pensionikeskus e-service: see when you got your first III pillar units. Pensionikeskus
  • In the III pillar overview of your bank or Tuleva account.
  • If you do not know, choose “2021 or later”. The calculation then does not count a lower income tax that you do not have.
futureMe.help.fundCur.title: What does the expected return mean?
futureMe.help.fundCur.body:
It is the fund’s yearly growth after fund fees but before inflation. The calculation itself takes off 2%, which the calculation assumes for yearly price rises.

Example: you pick 5%. Prices rise 2%, so in a year you can buy about 3% more than today.

  • 0%: the calculation starts here, because returns are not guaranteed. Prices still rise, so the assets buy less.
  • Below 2%: prices rise faster than the fund grows, and the assets buy less. This can happen when assets sit in a deposit or a fund falls for several years.
  • Above 2%: the fund grows faster than prices. The higher the return you pick, the bigger the risk that reality falls short of it.

The fee depends on how the fund is managed:

  • Index fund tracks a market index and does not pick individual securities. The fee is usually low.
  • Actively managed fund: a manager picks the securities. The fee is usually higher, and it cannot be known in advance whether the manager will beat the market.

The risk depends on what the fund holds:

  • Equity fund invests in shares. The risk is high: the price swings a lot and can fall for several years.
  • Bond fund invests in bonds. The risk is lower, but the return can fall short of price rises.
  • Mixed fund invests in both shares and bonds. The risk sits between the two and depends on the share of equities.

You can see the actual return, fee and risk level of each fund on the Pensionikeskus website. There you can filter funds with “Index funds”, “Actively managed funds” and “Risk level” (Low, Medium, High). Pensionikeskus returns are also before inflation and after the fund manager’s fees, so you can pick them here as they are.

Source: Pensionikeskus: II pillar fund returns and fees, Pensionikeskus: III pillar fund returns and fees.

World stocks returned about 5% a year after inflation on average in 1900–2024 (UBS Global Investment Returns Yearbook 2025). With prices rising 2% a year, that matches about 7% before inflation. Years differed a lot, and falls often come just before payouts. Past returns do not guarantee future returns.

You choose the II and III pillar returns separately, because the funds may differ.

Future Me shows amounts in today’s euros by default, so you can compare them with today’s prices. On the result chart you can also see them in future prices. The return is an assumption, not a promise.
futureMe.help.pillars.title: Why do we ask about your pillars and work?
futureMe.help.pillars.body:
From these details the calculation works out how much money you will have in your pillars at retirement age and how long it will last.

  • The II pillar is the mandatory funded pension: part of your salary and of the state’s social tax goes into a pension fund. You can use the money from 5 years before retirement age. You can take it out earlier only once, with 22% income tax (see the “II pillar contribution” explanation).
  • The III pillar is voluntary: you pay in yourself and get income tax back (up to 15% of your gross income, up to €6,000 a year).
  • Your gross salary sets your II pillar contribution and how much working at retirement age raises your pension.

Read more: Tuleva, Pensionikeskus, Social Insurance Board.
futureMe.help.special.title: Which special cases linked to work affect your pension?
futureMe.help.special.body:
Tick the ones that apply to you. Each tick opens its own questions; the others stay hidden.

a separate pension before retirement ageat retirement age you choose one: the special pension or the old-age pension (usually the larger)

Only one state pension is paid at a time. If you are entitled to several, you have to choose which one to use. The choice can change with age.

You have to choose one:

  • Special pension and old-age pension: before retirement age you get the special pension. At retirement age you choose which one you get: usually people choose the larger. Future Me picks the larger by default, but you can choose yourself.
  • Special pension and an earlier old-age pension for health-damaging work: if both are possible at the same age, you choose one. Oil shale mining and processing can give the right to either.
  • Old-age pension with the rescue service increase and special pension: at retirement age you choose one, usually the larger.

Apply together:

  • Children’s benefits (retiring earlier, pension supplement) add up with all of them. But the years earlier for children and for health-damaging work do not add up: the one that gives more years applies.
  • The list 1 supplement and the rescue service increase are added to the old-age pension, not the special pension.
  • The II and III pillar always add up: you get them next to any state pension.

If you have several special cases at once, check your rights with the Social Insurance Board.
futureMe.help.sp.title: What is a special pension?
futureMe.help.sp.body:
A special pension is a pension for certain occupations, paid under a separate law and often before retirement age. It is a state pension (I pillar).

  • Office pension: member of the defense forces (from 50 years, 20 years of service), police officer, prosecutor, judge, member of the Riigikogu, Chancellor of Justice, Auditor General.
  • Long-service pension: e.g. pilot, seafarer, ballet dancer, rescue worker, prison officer.

New employees no longer earn an office pension. The right belongs to those who were in office on the cut-off date: judges 1 July 2013; defense forces, police and prosecution 31 December 2019; rescue workers and prison officers 30 June 2022.

Service for a long-service pension counts until 31 December 2030 in occupations that require 10 or 12.5 years of service, and until 31 December 2036 in occupations that require 15–25 years. In oil shale mining, processing and enrichment, until 31 December 2049.

How it differs from health-damaging work: a long-service pension is a separate pension paid before retirement age because your ability to work in the occupation has declined. Health-damaging work (pension under favorable conditions) is an ordinary old-age pension taken earlier. Both have an oil shale exception until 2049, but only one is paid at a time: you choose.

How big it is: for the defense forces and the police, 50% of the official salary for 20 years of service, plus 2.5% for each extra year, up to 75% in total. You can see a special pension already granted in the Social Insurance Board self-service; work out the future amount yourself by this rule.

Two state pensions are not paid at the same time. When you reach retirement age (or the age for the children’s benefit), you can choose the larger: the special pension or the old-age pension. A special pension cannot be postponed, taken earlier or suspended.

Sources: Social Insurance Board: special pensions; cut-off dates for office pensions: the laws of each occupation. Data as of 26 October 2026.
futureMe.help.spStart.title: Why does the start of your special pension matter?
futureMe.help.spStart.body:
A special pension can start much earlier than the retirement age, for example at 50 for a member of the defense forces. From that age you get extra income.

The rules of the old system apply. Many special pensions are transitional provisions: they go to those who took office or met the conditions before the law changed. Those who started later get the ordinary pension rules. Your employer or the Social Insurance Board can tell you whether you are entitled, from what age and by which formula. Future Me assumes you know the amount of your special pension and the age it starts.

  • Working in another field is no obstacle: you get a salary and a special pension at the same time. Contributions from your salary keep going into the II pillar.
  • While working in the same office (or one treated as equal to it), the special pension is not paid (e.g. police officer, member of the defense forces, rescue worker, prison officer, judge, prosecutor). Enter the age you leave that office as the start. For example, a defense forces special pension is not paid while you work in the police, and a police special pension is not paid while you are in active service in the defense forces.
  • If you already receive a special pension, enter the age it started. Your earlier contributions are already in today’s amount of your II and III pillar.

The start age adds a special pension step to your path.
futureMe.help.hazard.title: What is health-damaging work?
futureMe.help.hazard.body:
If you have worked in particularly hard or health-damaging work on a list approved by the state, you get an old-age pension under favorable conditions. It is an ordinary old-age pension, not a special pension. It gives two benefits:

1. Retiring earlier without a reduction: list 1 up to 10 years, list 2 up to 5 years earlier. You can also go fewer years earlier: choose that in the “How many years earlier do you plan to retire?” field.

2. Pension supplement (list 1 only): each year of list 1 work adds 3.1% of the yearly rate to your pension (about €0.32 a month). That is why the calculation asks how many years you worked in listed work. A year of underground work adds a further 21.9% of the yearly rate (about €2.29 a month), but underground work does not lead to earlier retirement: the conditions are the same as for list 1 work. List 2 work counts as working years like any other work, but gives no supplement.

Conditions:

Since 2015 the conditions are the same for women and men.

The work had to be full-time. You get the pension under favorable conditions once you no longer do that work. You can keep doing other work. Listed work counts towards your length of service until 31 December 2030 (oil shale mining and processing until 31 December 2049).

Where to see the lists: Government Regulation No. 206 of 16 July 1992 approving the lists of industries, jobs, occupations and positions that give the right to an old-age pension under favorable conditions (Riigi Teataja, in force until 31 December 2030). The lists are by industry, for example mining, the chemical industry, metalworking and work with radiation. The lists are applied strictly: if your job is not on them, you have no right. The Social Insurance Board can tell you whether your work counts.

Future Me only checks your years of listed work: if you have fewer than 10 on list 1 or fewer than 12.5 on list 2, retiring earlier because of listed work is not counted. Future Me does not check your total length of service or other conditions: it assumes you know your length of service. The Social Insurance Board can tell you whether you are entitled.

If you also have a children’s benefit: when you have both, the one that gives more years earlier applies; the years do not add up.

Oil shale mining and processing can give the right either to this (an earlier old-age pension) or to a long-service pension (see “Special pension”). These are two different laws and only one is paid at a time: you choose; the Social Insurance Board can tell you which is larger.

Source: Social Insurance Board: old-age pension under favorable conditions, Old-age Pensions under Favourable Conditions Act § 1, lists 1 and 2 (Government Regulation No. 206). Data as of 26 October 2026.
futureMe.help.rescue.title: What does the rescue service give your pension?
futureMe.help.rescue.body:
The Rescue Service Act gives two benefits:

1. Leaving work earlier: if you have at least 15 years of rescue service, you can stop working up to 5 years before retirement age. Until retirement age the rescue agency pays you an allowance equal to your old-age pension including the increase. In the law it is called the “allowance for a rescue worker awaiting an old-age pension”; here we call it the waiting allowance. It is not paid if you keep working as a rescue worker. At retirement age the Social Insurance Board continues paying the old-age pension. Future Me cautiously assumes no social tax is paid on the allowance, so without paid work no contributions go into the II pillar.

2. An increase of the old-age pension by length of rescue service:

The increased pension is paid after you leave the rescue service. The increase provision applies until 28 February 2043: under the current text of the law, those who retire later do not get it. Future Me counts the increase if you retire in 2042 at the latest.

If you also get a special pension (a long-service pension), you choose at retirement age which one you get: usually the larger. The Rescue Board confirms your length of service.

Source: Rescue Service Act § 18 and § 19. Data as of 17 October 2026.
futureMe.help.civil.title: Who gets a pension increase for civil service?
futureMe.help.civil.body:
Civil Service Act § 113 is a transitional provision. The old-age pension increase goes to:

  • those who were already receiving it before 1 April 2013;
  • those who had the required years of service under the old Civil Service Act by 1 April 2013;
  • those who continued in service on favorable terms: their service counted for another 5 years, until 2018.

Those who became civil servants later do not get this increase.

futureMe.help.soodusYears.title: What happens if you retire earlier?
futureMe.help.soodusYears.body:
There are two ways to retire earlier:

1. Under favorable conditions, without a reduction. Because of children (3+ children or a child with a disability) or health-damaging work you can retire earlier and your state pension is not reduced. With at least 15 years of rescue service you can stop working up to 5 years earlier, and the rescue agency pays you an allowance equal to the old-age pension until you reach retirement age. The monthly pension is still slightly smaller, because you have fewer working years: with a €4,000 salary about €12 a month for each year. In total, though, you usually get more, because the pension is paid for longer (see below). In the Social Insurance Board calculator: 3 children (1 year earlier) €853, 4 children (3 years) €829, 5 children (5 years) €805 instead of the usual €865.

2. The flexible pension earlier, with a reduction. The flexible pension means you choose when to start your state pension: up to 5 years earlier, and the pension is smaller for life, or later, and it is larger for life. If you have no favorable conditions or go earlier than they allow, you can go up to 5 years earlier, but your state pension is reduced for life:

EarlierReduction1 year2 years3 years4 years5 years
−7.17%

The reduction is applied to the pension after the missing working years are taken off. For example, 3 years earlier: (€865 − 3 × €12.2) × (1 − 19.88%) = €664, as in the Social Insurance Board calculator. If you go earlier than favorable conditions allow, the reduction applies to all the earlier years.

Retiring earlier under favorable conditions usually gives you more state pension in total: going a year earlier gives you 12 months of extra pension (e.g. 12 × €853 ≈ €10,200), while the smaller monthly pension costs about €2,700 over the next 19 years. The flexible pension reduction, however, lasts for life, so with a long life you get less in total.

A right is not an obligation: you can also go later, up to the normal retirement age.

Source: State Pension Insurance Act § 10, Old-age Pensions under Favourable Conditions Act § 1, Rescue Service Act § 19, Social Insurance Board pension calculator, flexible pension. Data as of 16 October 2026.
futureMe.help.kids.title: How do children affect your pension?
futureMe.help.kids.body:
Prefilled children: those who have a Tuleva account. Children are not fetched from the population register; add other children yourself.

How Future Me counts children: each child separately, if by the time you retire you have raised them for at least 8 years (until the child turns 18). You can also enter the birth year of a future child. A child who turns 8 only after you retire is not counted. A child without a birth year is not counted.

Raising a child (for at least 8 years) gives two separate rights. One parent can use both rights for all the children, but the parents can also share them. The parents agree in writing; without an agreement the right is shared equally.

  • The other parent’s consent is not needed if they have died, if their parental rights were removed before the child turned 8, or if their place of residence cannot be found in the population register.
  • The agreement and the application are sent to the Social Insurance Board by email or in the self-service.
  • It is worth thinking about who gains more from the right: for example, the pension supplement is not added to a special pension, so the other parent could use it.

1. Retiring earlier without a reduction:

  • 3 children: 1 year earlier
  • 4 children: 3 years earlier
  • 5 or more children or a child with a disability: 5 years earlier

Your state pension is not reduced as it is when you take the flexible pension early (up to −30.7%). The monthly pension is still slightly smaller, because you have fewer working years, but in total you usually get more state pension, because it is paid for longer. If you also start II pillar payouts earlier, that monthly payout is smaller too: there are fewer contributions and the money is spread over a longer time.

In total you usually get more state pension, because it is paid for 1–5 years longer. For example, 3 children, 1 year earlier: the monthly pension is about €12 smaller (about €2,700 over 19 years), but the extra year of pension is about €10,200.

You can keep working. As long as you do not take money out of the II pillar, your and the state’s contributions keep going in next to your state pension. If you apply for II pillar payouts (including monthly payouts), contributions stop a few months later: on 31 August, 31 December or 30 April, depending on when you apply. In the retirement step (your retirement age on the path, e.g. “63”), answer “Will you keep working while you get your pension?” with “I keep working”. II pillar payouts start when your work ends if you choose “I take it monthly” (or “I take it all out”). You make this choice 5 years before retirement age (the step with that age on the path; if you retire 5 years earlier, the “pillars” step). If you choose “Keep saving” there and retire later, the calculation asks again in the retirement step. If you leave the money in the fund to grow, no payouts start.

Source: Pensionikeskus: II pillar payouts. Data as of 26 October 2026.

2. Pension supplement:

  • child born 1991–2012: 3.5 yearly rates (1.5 + 2)
  • child born before 1991: 1.5 yearly rates + 2 years of service (a year of service is worth the same as a yearly rate), also 3.5 in total
  • child born in 2013 or later: the state pays 4% of the Estonian average monthly income (2026: €76.12, 2027: €80.76 a month) into one parent’s II pillar until the child turns 3. If additional contributions were paid for fewer than 36 months (e.g. you joined the II pillar later), you get part of the pension supplement for the remaining months: for example, 12 months of additional contributions give 2/3 of the supplement (State Pension Insurance Act § 24 (6)).
  • without a II pillar, 3.5 yearly rates:
    • for a child born from 2013 to August 2021, if you were born before 1983;
    • for a child born in September 2021 or later, if you were not in the II pillar during the child’s first three years.

From 1 April 2026 the yearly rate is €10.48 a month. For example, two children born 1991–2012 give about €73 a month.

The supplement is not added to a special pension. If a special pensioner switches to the old-age pension at retirement age, the supplement is added to that.

Source: Social Insurance Board: raising children and your pension, State Pension Insurance Act § 24 (1¹) and § 28, Funded Pensions Act § 10. Data as of 26 October 2026.
futureMe.help.household.title: What changes if you live alone in retirement?
futureMe.help.household.body:
Living alone, your costs per person are higher: you pay for your home and bills by yourself. Living as a couple, the amounts are your share of the couple’s costs.

Allowance for a pensioner living alone: €200 once a year, with the October pension. It goes to a person of retirement age who lives alone according to the population register and whose net pension is under €992 a month (2026). You do not need to apply; the Social Insurance Board pays it automatically. It is not paid to someone living in a care home. The calculation does not add this allowance (about €17 a month).

Source: Social Insurance Board: allowance for a pensioner living alone. Data as of 26 October 2026.

futureMe.help.legacyLeft.title: How is this amount worked out?
futureMe.help.legacyLeft.body:
• Average life expectancy is the age that half of people your age live to (Statistics Estonia life table, your sex and birth year).
  • The amount is the money you have in funds and on deposit in total at the start of that year: all payouts so far are deducted and the return is added. The amount is in today’s euros.
  • Why it can be large: the monthly payout is the fund amount divided by your remaining life expectancy, so what is left in the fund keeps growing by the return. If the payout is bigger than your costs, the surplus builds up on the deposit.

Half of people your age live longer, so the money has to last beyond that age too.
futureMe.help.nominal.title: What does “future prices” show?
futureMe.help.nominal.body:
Normally all amounts are shown in today’s euros: €1,000 in 2045 buys as much as €1,000 today. This makes it easy to compare with today’s prices.

In future prices, the chart, table and summary look the way the amounts will really look in your account in future. The calculation assumes prices rise 2% a year (the European Central Bank’s target). For example, €1,500 of costs today is about €2,230 in 20 years. In the same way, €600,000 in your pillars is about €1.15 million in future euros in 33 years, but it buys as much as €600,000 today.

  • The result does not change: whether the money lasts, and to what age, is the same in both views. Only the way the amounts look changes.
  • What it is good for: you see why a bigger number in future does not necessarily mean more money, and later you can compare it with an amount you see in your bank account or in a Social Insurance Board notice. You will find the same view in the Tuleva pension calculator.
Rising prices are an assumption, not a forecast. The real pension is indexed every year and salaries rise, which the model in today’s euros does not show.
futureMe.help.kidIIMonths.title: How many months did the state pay into your II pillar for the child?
futureMe.help.kidIIMonths.body:
The state pays an additional contribution into a parent’s II pillar for the first 36 months of a child born in 2013 or later. The additional contribution is paid for each child separately and into one parent’s II pillar at a time. Enter how many months (0–36) the state paid the additional contribution into your II pillar for this child.

  • 36: you were in the II pillar for all of the child’s first three years.
  • 0: you were not in the II pillar at that time, so the state paid no additional contribution.
  • A number in between: you joined or left the II pillar during the child’s first three years.

The prefilled number comes from your II pillar contributions. The field stays empty if no state’s additional contributions were found, if the child is not yet 3, or if your children were born less than 3 years apart: the additional contribution does not say which child it was paid for. In that case, find the number in your Pensionikeskus II pillar statement or leave the field empty.

Why do we ask? For a child born in September 2021 or later, the parent’s supplement to the state pension depends on it: the fewer months the state paid into the II pillar, the larger the part of the supplement added to your pension.

futureMe.help.sustainable.body:

    {hasSpecialPension, select, yes {

Your costs are {need} a month. If your costs are lower than this amount, money is left over; if higher, your pillar money runs out sooner.
futureMe.help.rescueBasis.title: Waiting allowance or pension for children?
futureMe.help.rescueBasis.body:
If you are entitled both to the rescue worker’s waiting allowance and to retiring earlier because of children, you get one at a time: the waiting allowance is not paid if you already get a state pension.

The waiting allowance is not a pension. The rescue agency pays it at the level of the old-age pension (with the rescue worker’s increase). The children’s pension supplement is part of the old-age pension, paid by the Social Insurance Board. That is why Future Me counts cautiously: the children’s supplement is not added to the waiting allowance, it starts with the old-age pension.

The II pillar during the waiting allowance: the calculation also cautiously assumes no social tax is paid on the waiting allowance. If you do not work, no contributions (your 2–6% and the state’s 4%) go into the II pillar. The money keeps growing in the fund.

  • You raise the children alone: the children’s rights (retiring earlier and the pension supplement) stay with you. The pension for children also gives the pension supplement straight away.
  • With a partner: you decide together. You can take the waiting allowance, and the other parent uses the right to retire earlier because of the children. You choose this next to the children: “Who will use the right to retire earlier?”.
  • Both, one after the other: if the children give you, for example, 3 years earlier, you get 2 years of waiting allowance and then, 3 years before retirement age, the old-age pension for children with the children’s supplement.
futureMe.help.careHome.title: How is the cost of a care home split?
futureMe.help.careHome.body:
A care home place costs about €1,600 a month on average. It has two parts:

  • The care cost (about €600–730) is paid by the local authority for everyone, whatever your income.
  • The own share (accommodation and food) is yours to pay: about €750 in a cheaper place, about €950 on average and about €1,050 a month in a more expensive one.

On top of that, €100–150 a month can go on medicines, nappies and services (hairdresser, foot care). Some care homes include these in the price; ask for the price list.

If your money does not last, your adult children pay the missing part (a maintenance obligation under the law). If you have no family or the family cannot pay, the local authority helps, but you have to apply for support. The National Audit Office estimates that the pension of every third care home resident does not cover the own share.

Sources: ERR November 2025 (average place fee €1,603, 228 care homes), care home price lists 2025–2026, National Audit Office 2025.
futureMe.help.kidsSupUser.title: What is the pension supplement and how can it be shared?
futureMe.help.kidsSupUser.body:
The pension supplement is added to the old-age state pension for each child you have raised for at least 8 years. The person raising the child can be a parent (including an adoptive parent), a parent’s spouse or partner, or a guardian.

One parent gets the supplement. If the parents have not agreed in writing who gets it, it is shared equally between them.
futureMe.help.kidsIIUser.title: Who gets the state’s additional contribution to the II pillar?
futureMe.help.kidsIIUser.body:
Until the child turns 3, the state pays an additional contribution for them into one parent’s II pillar: 4% of the Estonian average monthly income (€76.12 a month in 2026). The parent who applies gets the additional contribution, and the other parent confirms the application. The additional contribution is not split in half.

If the state paid for fewer than 36 months, the parent who got the additional contribution also gets the pension supplement for the missing months. This remainder can also be shared with the other parent, but Future Me counts it as a supplement to your state pension if you got the additional contribution.
futureMe.help.kidsEarlyUser.title: Who can retire earlier because of children?
futureMe.help.kidsEarlyUser.body:
If you have raised three or more children, or a child with a disability, for at least 8 years, you can retire earlier without a reduction of your state pension: 3 children 1 year, 4 children 3 years, 5 or more children or a child with a disability 5 years. The person raising the child can be a parent (including an adoptive parent), a parent’s spouse or partner, or a guardian.

One parent uses the right. Without a written agreement, each parent gets half of the time, for example 6 months earlier each for 3 children. Future Me counts whole years only.
futureMe.help.kidDisabled.title: What does raising a child with a disability give?
futureMe.help.kidDisabled.body:
If you have raised a child with a moderate, severe or profound disability for at least 8 years, you can retire up to 5 years earlier without a reduction of your state pension.

The calculation uses this for your retirement age and the result.
futureMe.help.p3OpenAge.title: Why only up to retirement age?
futureMe.help.p3OpenAge.body:
Future Me counts payouts from retirement age, so here you can start up to retirement age. This is a limit of the app.

In real life you can also open a III pillar at retirement age and, depending on your situation, use the tax benefit too.
